title: JOHN THE BAPTIST WOULD RATHER LOSE HIS HEAD THAN REWRITE GOD’S STANDARD
paragraphs: JOHN THE BAPTIST WOULD RATHER LOSE HIS HEAD THAN REWRITE GOD’S STANDARD

They could imprison the preacher. They could silence his voice. They could even separate his head from his body. But they could not make John call sin holy—and the question haunting the Church today is whether we still have that kind of courage.
There was a head on a platter.
But before there was a platter, there was a prison.
Before there was a prison, there was an offended ruler.
And before there was an offended ruler, there was one sentence John the Baptist refused to soften.
“It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.”
That sentence cost him everything.
Read it slowly, because this is not merely an ancient story about a strange prophet, a corrupt palace, an angry woman, and a weak ruler.
This story walks uncomfortably close to us.
Because somewhere between John’s prison cell and Herod’s banquet hall is a question every generation of Christians eventually has to answer:
What happens when obedience to God starts costing you something?
Not when Christianity gets you encouragement.
Not when quoting Scripture earns applause.
Not when your convictions happen to agree with the people around you.
What happens when biblical truth costs you approval?
A friendship?
A relationship?
An opportunity?
Followers?
Income?
Reputation?
Comfort?
What happens when telling the truth could put something you love on the chopping block?
John had already answered.
Mark tells us that Herod Antipas had John arrested and imprisoned because of Herodias, whom Herod had married. John had confronted him concerning that relationship.
The Greek preserves the force of John’s words:
Οὐκ ἔξεστίν σοι ἔχειν τὴν γυναῖκα τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ σου.
Ouk exestin soi echein tēn gynaika tou adelphou sou.
“It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.”
Notice what John did not say.
He did not say, “Personally, I would have made a different choice.”
He did not say, “This lifestyle simply isn’t for me.”
He did not say, “We all interpret these things differently.”
He did not survey the palace to determine which version of truth would offend the fewest people.
He said:
Οὐκ ἔξεστίν.
“It is not lawful.”
Why?
Because John did not believe he possessed the authority to rewrite what God had spoken.
The background reaches into the Torah. Leviticus 18:16 says:
עֶרְוַת אֵשֶׁת־אָחִיךָ לֹא תְגַלֵּה
‘ervat eshet-achikha lo tegalleh.
“You shall not uncover the nakedness of your brother’s wife.”
John was not inventing morality according to his personality.
He was standing beneath a Word greater than himself.
And that distinction matters enormously.
Biblical courage is not shouting your personal opinions more aggressively than everybody else.
Biblical courage is submitting yourself to God’s Word first—and then refusing to pretend God said something different simply because obedience has become expensive.
John was not the author of the standard.
He was its messenger.
That is why the title of this story must never become an excuse for cruelty.
John’s courage does not authorize Christians to become arrogant, vicious, self-righteous, or obsessed with condemning everybody else.

The same Bible that calls sin sin commands us to speak truth in love. The same Jesus who preached repentance welcomed sinners who came to Him. The same Gospel that exposes rebellion announces forgiveness to rebels.
Truth without love becomes a weapon in the hands of proud people.
But love without truth becomes permission to continue walking toward destruction.
Jesus gives us something better.
Grace and truth.
And John understood something our age desperately needs to recover:
You do not love someone by lying to them about what God has said.
Imagine that prison cell.
Stone walls.
Chains.
Darkness.
Perhaps footsteps occasionally approaching through the corridor.
John—the wilderness preacher who once stood beside the Jordan with crowds gathering around him—is now confined.
The voice that cried in the wilderness is behind bars.
And here is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Because John could have changed his situation with something remarkably simple.
He did not necessarily need an army.
He did not need to overpower the guards.
He only needed to change his message.
Imagine how easy compromise could have sounded.
“Maybe I was too harsh.”
“Maybe I should have kept that part private.”
“Maybe Herod’s situation is complicated.”
“Maybe truth needs updating when powerful people dislike it.”
“Maybe survival matters more than faithfulness.”
Haven’t we heard versions of those whispers ourselves?
Maybe nobody needs to know.
Maybe Scripture doesn’t really mean that.
Maybe God understands.
Maybe repentance can wait.
Maybe obedience is too costly right now.
Maybe everybody does it.
Maybe if I call it something different, it will stop being sin.
But changing the vocabulary does not change reality before God.
And John refused to purchase freedom by selling truth.
Yet there is something even more disturbing in Mark’s account.
Herod listened to him.
Scripture says Herod feared John because he knew him to be righteous and holy. Herod was perplexed by him, yet he still liked listening to him.
Think about that.
A man can enjoy hearing a preacher he refuses to obey.
A person can admire holiness while refusing repentance.
You can listen to sermons.
Watch Christian videos.
Share Bible verses.
Cry during worship.
Follow Christian pages.
Feel convicted.
Even enjoy being convicted...
and still protect the very thing God is telling you to surrender.
Herod proves that fascination with truth is not the same thing as submission to truth.
And suddenly this is no longer merely Herod’s story.
It is ours.
There are people who want Jesus close enough to comfort them but never close enough to contradict them.
We want Christ as Savior but resist Him as Lord.
We want grace without repentance.
Forgiveness without surrender.
Resurrection without crucifixion.
A crown without a cross.
But Jesus never came merely to decorate the life we already chose.
He came to save us from sin and make us new.
That means the Gospel will eventually confront something in us.
Our pride.
Our lust.
Our bitterness.
Our dishonesty.
Our unforgiveness.
Our greed.
Our secret habits.
Our relationships.
Our idols.
Our desperate hunger for human approval.
And when Christ puts His finger on the thing we have been defending, we discover whether we really want Jesus—or merely the parts of Jesus that make us comfortable.
Then came the banquet.
Power gathered around tables.
Officials.
Commanders.
Influential men.
Food.
Entertainment.
Status.
Applause.
Herodias’s daughter danced, and Herod made a reckless promise before his guests.
Then came the request.
John’s head.
The Gospel tells us Herod became deeply distressed.
That detail matters.
His conscience was not completely silent.
He knew something was terribly wrong.
But he had made promises in front of important people.
And now Herod faced his own moment of decision.
John had already chosen God’s approval over a king’s approval.
Herod chose the approval of the room over obedience to what he knew was right.
Do you see the tragedy?
John was physically imprisoned...
but Herod was the greater prisoner.
John was chained to a wall.
Herod was chained to public opinion.
John could lose his head.
Herod could not bear losing face.
And there are prisons without bars.
The fear of being mocked.
The fear of being unfollowed.
The fear of losing friends.
The fear of being called intolerant.
The fear that family will misunderstand.
The fear that someone will leave if you finally obey God.
The fear of standing alone.
Some people will surrender their convictions before they surrender their reputation.
Herod shows us where that road can lead.
The executioner entered the prison.
There was no miraculous escape recorded.
No angel opened the door.
No earthquake shattered the chains.
John died.
That can trouble us because we sometimes confuse faithfulness with earthly success.
We imagine that if God is pleased with us, every faithful decision must produce an immediate happy ending.
But Scripture never promises that obedience will always preserve your comfort.
Sometimes obedience costs.
Sometimes righteousness is mocked.
Sometimes faithful witnesses suffer.
And eventually every disciple is confronted with Jesus’ words about denying self, taking up the cross, and following Him.
John’s death was not evidence that God had lost control.
Nor was John the Savior.
John himself had made that clear.
He was the voice preparing the way.
Jesus was the Lamb.
John said of Christ:
“Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!”
And here is where this story must ultimately take us.
Not merely to John’s courage.
To Jesus Christ.
Because Christianity is not ultimately the story of brave people trying harder to obey rules.
It is the story of guilty people who desperately need a Savior.
John confronted Herod’s sin.
But the Gospel confronts ours too.
If we finish this article thinking only, Yes, somebody needs to tell the world to repent, we may have missed the blade pointed toward our own hearts.
What does Jesus need to confront in you?
What have you renamed because repentance would hurt?
What relationship have you placed above Christ?
What hidden compromise survives because nobody knows?
What bitterness have you justified?
What secret appetite are you feeding?
What truth have you stopped saying because you desperately need people to like you?
What Scripture have you been negotiating with instead of obeying?
Do not answer quickly.
There are moments when God’s Word stops being information and becomes a mirror.
This may be one of them.
And if you see something ugly in that mirror, do not run away from Jesus.
Run to Him.
Because the center of Christianity is not a severed head on Herod’s platter.
It is the crucified and risen Christ.
Jesus did what John could never do.
John could announce repentance.
Jesus could purchase redemption.
John could identify sin.
Jesus carried sin to the cross.
John could point toward the Lamb.
Jesus was the Lamb.

At Calvary, the sinless Son of God bore judgment for sinners. He died and rose again, and everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith finds something Herod desperately needed and every one of us desperately needs:
Mercy.
Forgiveness.
A new heart.
A new allegiance.
A new life.
This is why biblical repentance is not God standing over broken people saying, “Clean yourself up before you approach Me.”
It is the sinner finally dropping the weapons of rebellion and coming empty-handed to Christ.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
But Jesus can redeem a surrendered life.
You cannot make your sins disappear by renaming them.
But Christ can forgive them.
You cannot save yourself by becoming religious enough.
But Jesus saves sinners who come to Him.
That is the scandal of grace.
Grace does not say your sin never mattered.

Grace says your sin mattered so terribly that Christ went to the cross—and that His mercy is so astonishingly great that the repentant sinner can be washed, forgiven, restored, adopted, and transformed.
From scandal to grace... because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by rewriting God’s standard.
By rewriting the sinner’s story.
That difference is everything.
Jesus does not need to redefine darkness to rescue someone from it.
He brings them into light.
He does not rename chains.
He breaks them.
He does not tell the guilty that guilt is imaginary.
He bears their guilt and offers righteousness they could never manufacture themselves.
So maybe the question is no longer whether John would lose his head rather than rewrite God’s standard.
We know his answer.
The question is:
What are you willing to lose rather than lose your faithfulness to Christ?
And perhaps an even deeper question:
What are you finally willing to surrender so Christ can have all of you?
Maybe your prayer is only three words.
“Jesus, forgive me.”
Not for performance.
Not because typing words earns forgiveness.
Only Jesus saves.
Let your comment simply become an honest confession that you do not want to hide anymore.
And then look through those comments.
You may discover someone else fighting a battle you understand.
Pray for them.
Encourage them.
Remind them of Christ.
This is what Christian community should look like—not perfect people displaying polished lives, but redeemed sinners pointing one another toward a perfect Savior.
And please do not keep this message trapped on this page.
Somebody on your Facebook friends list may be quietly negotiating with a sin that is destroying them.
Somebody may be terrified to obey God because obedience could cost a relationship.
Somebody may be living for the approval of the room like Herod.
Somebody may believe they have sinned too badly to return to Jesus.
Not to make yourself look spiritual.
There may come a day when compromise sounds reasonable and obedience feels painfully expensive.
Come back and remember the prisoner who would not rewrite the message just to escape the prison.
Supporting Gospel work is not a substitute for worship, obedience, generosity to your local church, or serving the people God has placed around you.
But the deepest reason to stay connected is not merchandise.
It is discipleship.
Truth.
Accountability.
Encouragement.
Spiritual nourishment.
A place continually calling us away from compromise and back toward Jesus Christ.

Because perhaps glorifying God today looks less like making a grand speech and more like refusing to be ashamed of Christ when one click could place biblical truth in front of someone who desperately needs it.
No livestream.
No microphone.
No algorithm.
He had a voice.
And when speaking cost him everything, he still refused to make God’s truth more convenient.
We have been given voices too.
May we use them with humility.
May we use them with compassion.
May we use them without self-righteousness.
May we use them without fear.
And above everything, may we use them to point people—not toward ourselves—but toward the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world.
Because one day every applause will fade.
Every follower count will become meaningless.
Every human opinion will fall silent.
Herod’s banquet ended.
The powerful men went home.
The platter disappeared.
Herod’s kingdom passed into history.
But the truth John refused to sell is still being preached.
And the Christ to whom John pointed is still saving sinners.
So when culture offers you applause in exchange for silence...
when compromise promises comfort...
when obedience becomes expensive...
when you are tempted to edit Scripture until it stops confronting you...
remember the prison.
Remember the banquet.
Remember the platter.
Remember John.
Then look beyond John to Jesus.
Repent where you have compromised.
Receive the grace Christ purchased.
Stand again.
Speak truth with love.
And follow the Lamb wherever He leads.
They could take John’s head, but they could never make him bow his conscience—and two thousand years later, his silence after death is still louder than Herod’s entire banquet.
